name: N-gram language models
statement: An n-gram model approximates the next word's distribution using at most n−1 preceding words. Estimate a continuation from its count divided by the total observed continuations of that context. Add-λ smoothing gives $P(w\mid h)=[c(h,w)+\lambda]/[\sum_xc(h,x)+\lambda V]$, a normalized distribution even for an unseen context. Without smoothing, a test continuation with zero support makes sequence probability zero and perplexity infinite. Perplexity is $2^{-\frac1T\sum_t\log_2P(w_t\mid h_t)}$.
idea:
More context can capture local word order but can also leave too little evidence. Interpolation mixes distributions from several context lengths; it differs from choosing a shorter order only when a longer one is missing. Neither higher order nor interpolation guarantees better test perplexity. Compare models on the same test tokens and vocabulary. Here interpolation uses an authored fixed weighting, including a positive uniform component; its weights are not fitted on the test data.

Choose a test-token position uniformly and let its context/next-word pair be the outcome. Within each observed context, cross-entropy (info 2.4) averages $-\log_2 q(w\mid h)$ under the empirical next-word distribution; averaging these conditional losses by the empirical context frequencies is exactly the displayed mean token log loss. Its exponential is perplexity. Any observed continuation with $q=0$ makes this loss and perplexity infinite. This finite test-set identity assumes neither independent test tokens nor convergence to a natural-language entropy rate, and it gives no guarantee that a higher-order model improves prediction.
caption: Choose the embedded Alice text, a small authored corpus, or your own text. Train on the first 85% of word tokens and evaluate every remaining token, with the test history initially empty. Select order and smoothing to highlight a point; both complete curves use the same train/test split. The generated 36-token sample uses exactly the selected probability distribution, including the explicit unknown token. Generate advances the saved seed.
scope: Finite continuous token streams across sentence boundaries; ASCII letters and internal apostrophes, lowercased, with curly apostrophes normalized. Training singletons and all test out-of-vocabulary words map to <unk>, which is always in the vocabulary. Early test positions use only the available history. Each context denominator is its outgoing count, excluding a terminal occurrence with no continuation. No sentence-boundary symbols or tuned practical smoothing are claimed. Alice is the repository's embedded Project Gutenberg11 text; the mini corpus is authored. Own text is limited to 10,000 characters with an explicit error.
refs: Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing, ch.3 §§3.1–3.6, official draft August 19, 2026
credit: Finite count illustration following Jurafsky and Martin.

name: Phrase-structure rules and syntax trees
statement: A context-free phrase-structure grammar rewrites one category at a time by productions such as S→NP VP. A finite ordered parse tree records which production expanded each category; its terminal yield is the generated sentence. The grammar defines a formal set of strings and their analyses. Describing a natural language requires empirical justification for those productions and may require devices beyond a CFG.
idea: Attach the ordered right-hand side of a production below the category it expands. Continuing until only terminals remain constructs a tree whose frontier is the derived string. Conversely, expanding an existing tree’s leftmost unexpanded category recovers a leftmost derivation. The actual CFG definition in TOC5.1 supplies this rewrite relation. A recognizer can prove that the typed word belongs to the supplied grammar, but a tiny grammar may undergenerate or overgenerate English, and a syntactically possible analysis can be pragmatically implausible.
caption: Edit the grammar and sentence, compute a real parse and replay its leftmost sentential forms. The final parse tree stays visible while the player changes the derivation. Try a missing lexical rule, a recursive rule, an empty production or a sentence outside the grammar.
scope: Editor limits:1800 grammar characters, 12 categories, 40 alternatives, eight symbols per right side, category names through eight characters and word tokens through 16. Typed sentences allow 12 tokens. Tree display limits are 85 nodes/depth 15; they do not turn a recognized word into a rejection.
refs: Jurafsky–Martin ch19 §§19.2–19.4; Richards MIT24.900 Lecture12, slides6–11 and47

name: Tarski’s definition of satisfaction
idea: Truth is defined by recursion on the formula, which is well defined by unique readability (logic-3.1). The quantifier clause cannot be phrased as “$\varphi$ is true”, because the body has a free variable; that is why satisfaction is defined for formulas *with an assignment*, and truth of sentences comes out as a special case. On a finite structure the definition is an algorithm. An $\exists$ needs one witness, and a false $\forall$ needs one counterexample. Read as a game, the Verifier picks witnesses for $\exists$ and the Falsifier picks counterexamples for $\forall$; $\mathfrak A\models\varphi$ exactly when the Verifier has a winning strategy.
caption: Draw a graph on the left (click a point and then another to toggle an arrow, click the same point twice for a loop), type a sentence and step through the evaluation. The player tries the elements one at a time for each quantifier, in order, and stops as soon as a witness (for $\exists$) or a counterexample (for $\forall$) settles it. Points hold chips for the current values of the variables, and the element being tried has an orange ring. In the tree, green means true and red means false for the current assignment. At the end the deciding element is marked, and the readout lists the witness for every $x$ or the counterexample.

name: The sorites paradox
statement:
Consider the predicate “is a heap of sand”, and these three claims.

(a) *Base case.* One grain of sand is not a heap.
(b) *Tolerance.* For every number $n$, if $n$ grains do not make a heap then $n+1$ grains do not make a heap: one grain cannot make the difference.
(c) *Clear case.* One million grains, suitably piled, make a heap.

By (a) and $999\,999$ applications of (b) with modus ponens, one million grains do not make a heap, contradicting (c). The argument is valid by ordinary logic, (a) and (c) look true, and each instance of (b) looks true. The same pattern works for any vague predicate whose application changes by small steps (*bald*, *tall*, *red*, *adult*).
idea: Something must give. Either some instance of the tolerance premise is false, so there is a sharp boundary somewhere between $1$ and $10^6$ grains; or an inference step is invalid; or the base or the clear case is not true; or the notion of truth itself needs revising. The sorites is a fixed point for the whole theory of vagueness: the following items of this chapter are the main answers (epistemicism, supervaluationism, degrees of truth), and the two later items explain why (b) tempts us. The puzzle is attributed to the Megarian philosopher Eubulides of Miletus (4th century BC), and its name comes from the Greek *soros*, “heap”. Formally, set S(n) to “n grains are not a heap”. The first principle of mathematical induction (alg-2.1) applies with base n=1 and the tolerance premise as its step, yielding S(n) for every positive integer n. This establishes the conditional consequence of those premises; it does not establish that tolerance is true of heaps.
caption: Drag the grain count $n$ to build the pile (a sample of at most 355 grains is drawn; the label gives the real count). Drag the green handle on the right to choose *your* cut-off $c$: the smallest number of grains you call a heap. With *tolerance accepted*, the chain of modus ponens steps from 1 grain reaches every $n$ and concludes that $n$ grains are not a heap, which contradicts your verdict as soon as $n\ge c$. Switch tolerance off and every instance of the premise is true except the single red pair $(c-1,c)$, a sharp boundary that one grain crosses.
credit: Attributed to Eubulides of Miletus, 4th century BC (SEP “Sorites Paradox”)

name: The Munsell colour system
statement: Munsell orders surface colours by hue, value and chroma. The renotation table associates these labels with colourimetric targets under illuminant C and the CIE 1931 2° observer. Its available chroma extent varies with hue and value; it is not a cylinder. These targets include interpolations and are not measurements of chips from a particular book.
idea: A value/chroma leaf makes the irregular extent visible without pretending that a continuous surface has been measured. Rotating a radial layout joins ten sampled hue leaves into an order diagram. The tree uses an authored oblique projection: x=C cos φ and y=V+0.018C sin φ. Its radial units are not CIELAB distances.
caption: Choose a hue and value, then a tabulated chroma. Switch between the selected leaf and a rotating tree of ten principal hues. The gold ring locates the actual selected table entry. Rendered chips use the declared illuminant adaptation and may clip.
refs: RIT Munsell Color Science Laboratory, Educational Resources, Munsell Renotation Data, real.dat
scope: All 2734 RIT real.dat rows are stored unchanged. The tree shows ten principal 5-hue leaves, values1–9, at their actual tabulated chromas. For preview only, source Y relative to smoked MgO is multiplied by0.975, converted from xyY, Bradford-adapted from C (x=.31006,y=.31616) to D65 and clipped to sRGB. This transform does not reproduce a physical Munsell chip.
viz:
viz(v){const mode=v.select('diagram',['leaf','tree'],'leaf'),H=v.select('hue',HUES,'5R'),V=v.slider('Munsell value',1,9,5,{int:true}),C=v.slider('chroma index',0,15,2,{int:true}),angle=v.slider('tree rotation (degrees)',0,360,25,{step:1}),s=v.stage({x:[-1,30],y:[0,10],axes:'box',gutter:true,height:400,xlabel:'Munsell chroma',ylabel:'Munsell value'}),p=patches(v,'selected renotation target');let row,rows;
v.render(()=>{rows=munsellRows(H.value,V.value);row=rows[Math.min(C.value,rows.length-1)];const tree=mode.value==='tree';angle.el.hidden=!tree;s.setView(tree?[-35,35]:[-1,34],[0,10]);s.setLabels(tree?'rotated radial coordinate':'Munsell chroma','Munsell value');if(tree){for(let hi=0;hi<10;hi++){const phi=(hi*36+angle.value)*Math.PI/180;for(const r of MUNSELL.filter(r=>r[0]===HUES[hi])){const x=r[2]*Math.cos(phi),y=r[1]+.018*r[2]*Math.sin(phi);s.dot(x,y,{color:munsellDisplay(r),r:3,ring:false});}}s.dot(row[2]*Math.cos((HUES.indexOf(H.value)*36+angle.value)*Math.PI/180),row[1]+.018*row[2]*Math.sin((HUES.indexOf(H.value)*36+angle.value)*Math.PI/180),{color:'gold',r:7});}else{for(const r of MUNSELL.filter(r=>r[0]===H.value)){s.rect(r[2]-.7,r[1]-.28,r[2]+.7,r[1]+.28,{fill:munsellDisplay(r),stroke:false,fillAlpha:1});}s.dot(row[2],row[1],{color:'gold',r:7});}patch(p,0,1,adapt(munsellXYZ(row),WC,D65));});v.readout(()=>`${row[0]} ${row[1]}/${row[2]}: source xyY=(${fmt(row.slice(3),5)})\n${rows.length} available chromas on this value row; index ${Math.min(C.value,rows.length-1)} (requested ${C.value}, clamped to available entries). Display Y=${(row[5]*.975/100).toFixed(6)}; ${inGamut(linearRGB(adapt(munsellXYZ(row),WC,D65)))?'inside':'outside'} sRGB.`);}
